It’s the easiest way to get both of my eyes, and all 8 of Tesla’s “eyes” (cameras), all searching for safety threats.

Thinking on it there are a lot of inputs at pickup and drop off humans take in and make decisions to make a better experience. A human can essentially know what experience they would like or what is most convienent for the passanger. I think Waymo's will improve on it but you just have to accept walking to a specific location and getting dropped off at a specific location then walk from there. I have no issue with it and loved my experience just some observations.

Author: @emilemil1
Content:
Personally I think robotaxis are very far away from being actually useful, at least in my city where public transportation or a bike are much cleaner and cheaper alternatives.

I only wish I had a car when I need to move something large or heavy, or when I need a ride out of town (possibly on uncharted dirt roads), or when I want a social trip with friends. If I could call a cheap robotaxi for these use cases then that'd be great.

But I'm sure we'll eventually get to a point where owning a personal car will be seen as superflous, which will be really nice since that means we'll be able to get rid of so many parking lots. Cars would also be made to not have a driver which would obviously cut costs since basically the whole front interface can be removed. Cars can also be made for specific purposes, you could for example have one that's just a big bed for long comfortable trips, one which is one seat and a big storage area for moving stuff, etc.

Author: @toddjohnson5692
Content: The biggest issue I think, is how to get these various vehicles to use the same 'signals' to decide what to do. For instance, we used FSD in a new Model Y to drive about 240 miles, mostly on the highway. We found that it did ok and for the most part avoided problems. It was a bit too cautious at times and clearly was programmed to not hog the left lane on the highway. The only real issue was on an exits that have multiple lanes. It didn't know which to pick and one might be just for a local pull off while the other was to go to an onramp of another highway. Until they can understand the signage (and sometimes even that is confusing to people), such things will need a driver to take control. But it handled road construction even with flag people and having to move to the other side of the road just fine. Making signage universal and readable by the self driving cars will be the biggest issue world-wide IMHO.

Author: @RealRadNek
Content: Marques, there was so much you missed to inform your audience.  Let me just scratch some of the surface for you.  A deeper dive would reveal a huge difference between Waymo & Robotaxi.  Tesla has billions of real mile training miles with millions of cars.  Because it is so difficult for Tesla to now get a car to learn from real life mistakes of drivers, they are now relying on AI generated videos for life threatening edge case scenarios like head on collisions so the system can keep learning.  Waymo has only 3500 cars on the road presently.  Do the math.   Waymo will always lag way behind Tesla as a result.  Waymo's solution requires a $50k-$80k car they must purchase from an OEM and retrofit with sensors to the tune of at least $50k in hardware +labor costs for retrofit.  It takes Tesla 2.5 hours to manufacture a robotaxi (model Y) start to finish for around $40k.  Tesla will be multiplying their self driving taxi fleet while Waymo continues to add cars here and there.  Do the math.  Who scales to 100k vehicles first?  With Cybercab, Waymo is in deeper trouble.  Tesla says that without paint and the unbox method, it will take 5 seconds to create a cybercab.   Not sure I believe that but let's say it takes them 10 minutes to manufacture 1 Cybercab @ about $20k-$25k per Cybercab.  Tesla's intention is to get their presently $1 per mile charge down to $0.50 per mile.  Do the math.  Waymo & Uber are cooked once the safety rider comes out of the car.  I do hope Waymo figures something out because like you said, competition is good but presently, it's not looking too good.

Author: @henrytuttle
Content:
I've ridden in FSD for weeks and had multiple critical interventions. I've been on top of this for years.

Tesla's tech is good... for a car without LIDAR. But they should have used LIDAR. I don't think vision without LIDAR will be as good as a system with LIDAR until AGI. And even if that happens soonish (within 5 years) I don't think Tesla's computers will be able to handle it and will require one or two generations better than the current onboard computers.

LIDAR on a Tesla would have raised the price by $3-5000. They could have easily done it. And the safety improvements would have been significant. There's just stuff that a computer can't do with vision that a person can For example, a black spot on the ground might be a hole or a shadow or something else.  A human would see an empty paint can next to it and understand it's spilled paint. The FSD won't understand that. LIDAR would know it's not a hole. Same thing with a reflection or a painting. Humans use context clues. Computers CAN, but not well yet.

I am a risk tolerant person (skydiving, etc.) I would ride in a car with Tesla FSD. But I wouldn't send it to pick up my kids. Both because I don't really trust it yet, and because in cases of minor problems, the kids would freak out.

Author: @Ducky-face
Content:
Robotic taxis - I call them Johnny-cabs in honor of Total Recall -  don't and are never going to make economic sense: the upfront purchase price of the vehicles, coupled with the massive amounts of liability insurance that will be required to operate them, balanced against what they could realistically charge for fares will never never add up to a profit. 
Under normal use the vehicles will be ready for the scrapyard long before the owner breaks even on the initial investment on the vehicle -let alone all of the other associated operating expenses and repairs - and there's no way to scale the production of these vehicles to avoid that outcome. Just because the technology kinda exists, does not mean it will ever be cost-effective to use this way.
Not to mention that pretty much no legislator expecting reelection is going to want the reputation among their constituents of being the "job-killer' who approved the use of these vehicles on local roads.
 Robotic vehicles are like communism; on the surface it might seem like a good idea, but unless EVERY vehicle on the road is robotic and attached to the same network -   meaning NO human drivers anymore - it simply can't work. There's never going to be a truly safe way to integrate these vehicles safely into typical urban traffic patterns without the vehicles costing unrealistic amounts of money; far too much to use as a taxi.

Author: @suisinghoraceho2403
Content:
Despite the glitches, the worst part about the RoboTaxi and the whole Tesla autonomous driving is the lack of transparency. Without which, no one can be sure really how good it is. Considering this: They have fired exactly zero raw test data with their test licence so far. Even Apple filed more.

One thing about deep neural network is that they behave like human and makes judgments on complex situations SUBJECTIVELY. Which means they no longer operates on the line of ‘if there are obstacles within certain parameters, do this’, and their responses could vary even if approaching exactly the same situation. Able to handle a situation this time around doesn’t mean they can do the same next time. So individual success and fails are just that and doesn’t mean anything. The only way you can know is by watching the trends in Data. And the only way to get the public to trust your conclusion is to publish the raw data and let the public draw their own conclusion. 

Sure, Waymo is probably not as transparent as it could be. But they are still light years ahead. Tesla’s lack of transparency is only hurting themselves in the long run: you risk letting individual incidents define your whole brand.

Author: @ChrisRuzin
Content:
I've seen Waymos all over the place for a long time in Austin. At first I thought they were ugly, gimmicky, and dangerous. Over the years I've watched them successfully navigate some really tricky traffic situations. I've seen them do things a more experienced driver would do like correctly yielding in unusual circumstances, creeping out into the intersection to wait for traffic before turning, navigate construction areas and human-directed traffic, and navigate heavy, unpredictable foot traffic at busy intersections. Honestly the Waymos seem better on the road than your average Austin driver. Now I no longer think they're gimmicky and seem a lot less dangerous than your average Austin driver. They're still ugly AF though.

The Robotaxis feel rushed out & half-baked in comparison. They're fairly new in Austin, so I haven't seen them around as much to see how they handle tricky situations. Having someone sitting up front, always holding the door handle says to me they are less confident in their product. I'm sure the experience will improve given enough time, but so will Waymo's.

Waymo clearly has had a LOT more time and experience, and it shows. If I had to choose between the two I'd choose Waymo without hesitation.

Author: @ÁlvaroDQ
Content: i dont agree with crtiticizing unilaterally the silly mistakes. Think about it this way. What do you prefer, having 5 people killed on accidents or having an autonomous car struggling to park the car sometimes with some people? Aside from the fact that these silly mistakes that a human would never do are pretty rare, if you compare that with accidents that kill people its nothing, its clearly an upgrade. We are already months in on the world in which is safer to ride an autonomous car than a human driven car. You can look up the statistics. Out of any X amount of miles driven, there are more accidents per mile in human driven cars than in autonomous cars. Yes, AI will make mistakes that a human would never do, weird silly bugs. But when the alternative is having double the people dying on accidents or being injured (and when i say double i dont care if its 1.2x, 1.5x, 2x, 5x, etc the point is that there are less accidents), i think we can all agree that we'd choose the autonomous 100 times out of a hundred. Remember, we are only months after having surpassed human driven car safety. It will keep getting safer than it is now even. So no, i wouldnt give relevance to those silly mistakes, unless i considered the silly mistakes and silly deaths that humans cause while driving. And also, its natural and organic that these AIs still are making silly mistakes. Think about it, you are Tesla, you get data from the cars of accidents and deaths and things like that and then you research those edgecases, update the AI over time, and fix gradually all the bugs that have been causing accidents. Then, the only bugs that wil be left will be the silly bugs that dont get anyone hurt. Because the ones that were fatal were prioritized and solved, so you end up with a pretty safe car that has mistakes that make people laugh because of how absurd they look. This is just that point in the road, the point in which we've solved majority of accidents but still havent solved the weird absurd harmless ones. In 2 years we wont be on that point on the road anymore, we will be ahead of that. So i dont see it as something that should be considered when thinking about how is the technology and the service and how it will evolve

Author: @juliahello6673
Content: The problem with Waymo is that the vehicles don’t figure out the landscape. The area is mapped repeatedly with high definition cameras. It’s like the cars are on invisible rails. Of course they have to do all sorts of remarkable things with other cars, pedestrians, animals, etc. But there is a huge chunk of cognition that they don’t have to do because they are pre-mapped. So what is wrong with this strategy? Two things . First, it’s expensive and cumbersome to map the entire area every few days. It works ok in smaller areas, but could Waymo map every road in the United States every few days? Well, maybe if they have a huge fleet of drones or something like that. But it doesn’t seem like a scalable solution and Waymo knows it and they have said that they need to move to a system more like Tesla’s. The second reason why high definition mapping and LIDAR don’t work so well is that the road may change in between mappings. What if construction is done? What if a rockslide or sinkhole takes out the road? Waymo has said that their strategy is to try to switch to a system like Tesla’s but the cofounder of Cruise was interviewed a few weeks ago and made a good point. He said that Waymo has already built and been approved for its current system, so trying to switch would mean that they backtrack on safety because anything new would be experimental and unpolished.

Author: @ericandi
Content:
I’ve had a Tesla Model 3 with FSD for 9 months. FSD is already a much safer driver than humans, me included, which is why, despite the fact that FSD occasionally drives a little differently than I would and makes some driving choices that I wouldn’t make, I let FSD drive 99% of the time because I know it’s much less likely to get in a accident that will kill or cause great bodily harm to me, my passengers, and/or other drivers on the road. 

As far as having to intervene and take over because of FSD doing something that’s unsafe, going the wrong way, or getting stuck in a weird situation, on average, I have to intervene and take over about every 750 to 1000 miles driven by FSD. I owned an FSD Tesla about 4 years ago and sold it about 2 years ago. At that time, I had to intervene about once every 50 miles. When I purchased my current Tesla last November before the big end of the year FSD software update, I had to intervene about once every 300 to 500 miles. 

FSD is clearly getting better and better with every update. It’s already a much better and safer driver than the average human driver, including me, because it never gets distracted, has a much faster response time, and can simultaneously see 360 degrees around the vehicle at all times. 

Humans are horrible drivers. Not because of a lack of driving skills, although for some people do have poor driving skill. Humans are primarily horrible drivers because of the reasons I listed. We are constantly distracted when driving. Even if we never talk on the phone while driving, pretty much everything a driver does while driving causes a distraction. 

Studies have found that when a driver talks to passengers, they suffer a decline in driving acumen and safety just as much as talking on the phone, whether holding a phone or via Bluetooth. Changing the radio station, AC, mirrors, seats, etc. also cause distractions and compromise safety. 

Even when a human isn’t distracted, once we identify something that requires us to react, we have slow reflexes and response times. Not to mention that we only have two eyes with a very limited field of view. We have mirrors but we can’t look forward and in our rear view mirror or side mirrors at the same time, not to mention the blind spots. When we are looking in our rear view mirror, our forward vision is nonexistent.


Tesla vision FSD has 8 cameras providing a continuous 360 degree view. The FSD computer can also recognize situations, decide what to do, and execute much faster than a completely focused, undistracted human driver. Once you add in all of the common distractions, FSD is far superior. 

Too many people get hung up on the minor things that FSD does differently than they would. Things like FSD driving a little too slow or too fast, staying in the slow lane or fast lane too long, or not getting in the turn lane soon enough. For the most part, these are all personal preferences. If you ask a hundred drivers they will all have different opinions and approaches to driving. I’m far more concerned with avoiding major accidents that will kill or injure me, my passengers, and other drivers and I know FSD is far better at that than I am.

Author: @martincday007
Content:
While Tesla advocates often resist acknowledging Waymo’s achievements, many who favour Waymo, and would prefer to seek a more balanced discourse, feel compelled to push back against Tesla’s self-proclaimed leadership in vehicle automation, which is not supported by the facts.

Tesla, largely through Elon Musk, consistently exaggerates the capabilities of its technology. The company not only lacks transparency in the aftermath of incidents but has actively obstructed efforts by law enforcement and regulators to access critical data.

In reality, Tesla is following the path Waymo pioneered, operating within geofenced, pre-mapped environments. A meaningful comparison between the two will only be appropriate once Tesla deploys a fleet of truly autonomous vehicles.

Importantly, Waymo’s primary competition isn’t Tesla, but ride-hailing platforms like Uber and Lyft. Removing the driver offers clear advantages, but it also introduces operational challenges, some of which are less obvious. One major drawback of fully autonomous fleets is the need to scale for peak demand, resulting in significant idle capacity during off-peak hours. Unlike Uber, whose vehicle overhead is absorbed by driver compensation, Waymo must bear the full cost of underutilised vehicles.

There is still some debate as to which model, RoboTaxi or Uber, is the most profitable.

Author: @MilesBellas
Content:
via PERPLEXITY

The geofence shape has gained notable attention for its provocative, phallic-like outline, which appears to be a deliberate, humorous, and somewhat bold message from Elon Musk aimed at competitors like Waymo. This expanded shape now even envelopes much of Waymo’s geofence area in Austin, indicating Tesla's aggressive market positioning and growth in its ride-hailing network. 
Key points about the Tesla Robotaxi geofence and shape:

The initial geofence (~20 sq mi) was rapidly expanded first to about 42 sq mi, then nearly doubled again to ~80-85 sq mi, showing Tesla’s confidence in their Robotaxi system for urban driving conditions in Austin.

The shape of the geofence is deliberately striking and resembles a phallic symbol, which elicited humorous and provocative reactions on social media, including from Elon Musk and Tesla’s official Robotaxi account.

The expansion overlaps and surpasses Waymo’s previously larger service region, positioning Tesla as a strong competitor in the autonomous ride-hailing market in Austin.

Tesla uses validation vehicles with sensor rigs including LiDAR for ground-truth validation of its camera-based vision system but continues to emphasize vision-only autonomous driving.

Content:
Neural networks need visual comprehension. Not only the stuff "rudimentary" neural networks are able to do, such keep a lane, know who is in front, behind, left and right , or having the reflexes to stop at possible dangers.

A neural network that drives a cab should be able to reply about everything you ask it while driving and give answers as a human would. It needs to have a presence, and be aware whom they are carrying, where they are carrying them to, what the behavior of passerby pedestrians and vehicles may implicitly mean, to anticipate behaviors before they manifest, have an ingrained appreciation for human life , even though many humans don't(while they do show hypocritical love to pets).

There was a time when even the performance of "rudimentary" neural networks was considered sci-fi and their possibility was a subject of extreme and long speculations. So , there is more probable than not , that AI will eventually be able to drive and surpass experienced cab drivers. 
It was not long ago, that self-driving cars was the subject of investigation and encouragement through government competitions and funds. Anyone remembers the DARPA challenges in the first decade of our century ?
Huge progress has been achieved since then.
The problem is not if it happens. The problem is what we do when it happens.

Author: @thisistechnologia
Content:
Let me tell you about some places in India🇮🇳 where this will be a real challenge to operate. 

There are some cities which have two types of cabs, one is online another is offline. Offline cabs are part of driver union and they just hate the convenience of online cabs. Obviously they have tried to operate online but in a saturated market you hardly get any passenger. So the offline cabs union they assign themselves some particular areas that they operate from which we have to visit and ask for a ride, like near railway stations or bus stands and they defend these areas from any online cabs, so any online cabs that pickup from these areas the driver is just beaten badly or his cab is damaged so by experience the online cab drivers just know which areas to avoid pickups from. So now you would think why would someone book a online cab when there are some right in front of you, online cabs are obviously cheaper because algorithm decides the rates based on demands but offline cab driver has a union so they are fixed at a particular rate and no one is allowed to negotiate or he will be removed from the union.

Now comes the part where this driverless cabs obviously won't know where to not pickup from and being driverless the vehicle will be the primary target so even if the roads are perfect and the traffic is less, there are variables like these which it has to face.

Author: @bmurphy666
Content:
Appreciate this (in most cases) fair & balance view.

I think what he gets wrong is that most people aren't picking sides & only hoping one team will win. Some might but most that I watch don't.

The fact is that most people can see the technological differences & how far ahead Tesla is. Have they got less cars & people in them. Of course they do because there are laws & requirements you need to meet before you can advance further. 

Also, it's easy to forget that of course Waymo is further ahead. They've had their AVs on the road 7 years longer than Tesla & have advanced at a snails pace because of the technological differences that are holding them back. TAM is big enough for both to succeed in some sort of capacity but will they? Will have to wait & see.

I also, noted that he didn't speak about the 2nd most important thing when it comes to AVs after safety & that's cost. He covered the cost to build the cars which is fine. Teslas are cheaper & safer to build & be involved in a crash but he didn't touch on cost per autonomous mile which is the only thing it's going to come down to.

Good luck to all.

Author: @JokingJay
Content:
15:33 That's the problem with Tesla in a nutshell: they do nothing "as safely and methodically as possible." It's more of a "move fast, break things" approach, in no small part because the CEO has been promising "full self driving" for literally a decade and has said that the future of the company hinges on it. That's the kind of pressure that leads one to cut corners, overstate FSD's capabilities, overlook anomalies, etc. And the recent case in Florida shows us that Tesla is willing to do all the above, cover it up, and even try to shirk responsibility when it's cost human lives.

Conversely, while Waymo is by no means perfect, their vehicles have been involved in a total of five accidents with "serious" injuries, one of which included a fatality -- and human drivers were at fault for all of them. The same cannot be said for Tesla's FSD by any stretch of the imagination, and yet they've put it out there as though it's ready. As such, I think it's flawed to equate the two services. Which is to say nothing about the miles between critical disengagement metric, which we know Waymo is far, far ahead in; indeed, they ostensibly don't have critical disengagements anymore, because there's no safety driver to take over in real-time (only teleoperation). Meanwhile, Tesla has and regularly makes use of their safety drivers. It's simply not comparable.

Content: One important point about the safety of autonomous vehicles is that because dangerous crashes are so rare, personal anecdotal experience is not actually all that useful in gauging how good it is. The sample size is just too small. For instance, when Tesla was doing a promotional free month of FSD, I tried it once on a ~10 mile trip and had zero interventions. I was really impressed until I remembered that the average crash happens every at the frequency of hundreds of thousands of miles. An entire lifetime of driving might not be enough to robustly assess whether you would have been better off driving yourself. So looking at the statistics really matters.

Author: @BLAISEDAHL96
Content:
15:48 Then explain how a Cruise robotaxi *dragged a pedestrian through an intersection* despite having all of the same sensors as a Waymo? I worked for Cruise from 2021-2024 and fundamentally disagreed with their methodology the entire time, nevertheless fascinated by what the technology was & is capable of. 

If you saw how insanely more complicated a Global B electrical architecture is compared to a Model Y, you'd be shocked. The Cruise Origin (purpose built robotaxi) main HV wire harness was nearly 200 lbs, if I recall. At the thickest point It had the same diameter as a small tree sapling. 

This pales in comparison to how insanely efficient Tesla's electrical design is. The vertical integration means more control over hardware, controllers & the firmware which operates & communicates betweeen them. I just trust the base vehicle way more than I do an EV made with outmoded electrical architectures. 

The same reason you can automatically connect your streaming app accounts to a Tesla robotaxi are the same reasons why I trust the base vehicle over a system like Waymo's which has far less vertical integration of hardware & software. 

I think you reaaaaaaaaaaaally don't like Elon Musk & are trying *hard* to be fair, which I appreciate.

Author: @colesonafrank5329
Content:
I sure wish Musk's character wasn't so accurately depicted by Austin's geofence.  Despite his infantile racism and fascist politics, Tesla's approach to FSD deserves far more credit than it's getting.  Why isn't it getting appropriate credit?  First because all the corporations the disrespectful upstart's empire are seriously disrupting have been waging an all out PR war against him  (being such a pathetically flawed and easy target).  And second, because his fundamental values regarding human life (predominantly contempt, as demonstrated through DOGE's actions) are antithetical to a sustainable civilization, so socially progressive folks stopped promoting anything associated with him.

Why does it deserve more credit?  It seems to me that Tesla's approach to FSD will, unless it gets horribly sabotaged, FAR outpace Waymo in every way, starting with it's rapid scalability.  It's first unsurmountable advantage is that all Teslas which are hardware compatible use an FSD system that is totally under AI control, from receiving and processing the sensory data from the cameras and all the car's control systems, through learning from such data being collected from almost the entire fleet of Tesla's ever sold (on roads all over the country and beyond), through integrating what it already remembers about its current situation (e.g. details along its route) with everything it's sensing as it drives and responding intelligently in real time.   Given the human monitor required as reasonable abundance of caution for such a consequential technological paradigm shift, in Tesla's case the geofencing is almost, but not quite here at the very beginning, superfluous.

The point being that Tesla's FSD is totally based on learning from cars all over the country and that with each update they all learn together, the time it would reasonably take from them to be allowed everywhere would be quite brief; the real delays will mostly be politically driven by the petrochemical-based companies.  While folks are encouraged to believe that fully autonomous vehicles "have" (or even should) be "perfect" before they should be allowed everywhere, that will unnecessarily kill and maim a bunch of people.  Humans' driving capabilities cover a broad spectrum, from truly appalling to rather astounding.  From my perspective human averages are anywhere from pathetic to pretty scary with success and survival depending largely on good fortune and luck.  Within the (aggregated and compounded) ranges of performance characteristics of all the cars' components, all the FSD Tesla's everywhere will perform as optimally as they all have learned.  Consistently, with plenty of but far fewer brain farts and stupid sensory lapses and mistakes, than humans.

The other huge reason that Tesla will scale far faster is that its cars are designed especially well to be efficiently mass produced at minimal cost.  And so are the factories which produce them.  Their cost advantage alone puts them way ahead of all (non-Chinese) competition.

The point is that these self driving vehicle services might be about the only way transportation needs can be met by those needing affordable ways to get around that are not slow or hard to find. 

If you can have all your monthly transportation needs met reliably and conveniently for $250 a month, that can greatly reduce the need or desire to own a vehicle.

The tech isn’t the issue, the issue is legal. So if that Tesla has an accident and kills someone because of the AI,

Who goes to gaol if it was a driverless car- Musk because he released software too early? Or who gets sued. We are seeing this happen in lots of court cases where people are having to fight a large litigious corporation for years often having to settle out of court. The thing is there is no physical reason a 14 year old couldn’t hold a drivers licence if they could pass the test.. but we don’t allow that for a very good reason- and it’s not because they are bad drivers. 

The big question is why are we doing all of this? Is it just so Tesla can make more money? As you say it’s interesting tech… but I’m left thinking it’s perhaps not the application of AI humans should be prioritising, just because it boosts share prices.

On the other hand Robotaxi is Tesla FSD, basically an ai that uses the same senses a human does to drive (primarily vision), which does not require hd maps to work, it just works everywhere a human would. Thanks to that, Robotaxi in weeks has more coverage than Waymo done in years and is only limited by governmental approval instead of need for creating hd maps of the areas.

Content:
The one thing people need to understand about how to measure safety of these services is not if they are perfect and never make a mistake, they will. It's if they ultimately result in less accidents than humans overall. There are over 40k fatal accidents per year in the US, millions worldwide. If Robotaxi/Waymo puts a significant dent in these numbers, this would still be a massive success for road safety.

And the cool thing about these technologies, is this is the worst they will ever be, they will only get better and safer from here. Cannot say the same about the average human driver who has not improved over the past while, and in fact has gotten worse recently due to texting. This technology will save lives and we should all be rooting for that.

Thanks for covering this Marques!
